newsitem.title: IRAQ: Russia in pole position for more Iraqi oilfields.
newsitem.headline: Russia in pole position for more Iraqi oilfields.

text.p: Russian oil companies have the chance to quickly follow up on their success last month in securing the rights to develop one of Iraq's biggest oilfields, diplomats and oil officials in Baghdad said on Wednesday.
Russian companies along with Chinese and French firms are leading the race to tie up oil deals with Iraq, the country which holds the world's second largest oil reserves behind Saudi Arabia.
Iraqi officials on Wednesday said ten developments were up for grabs with discussions also underway with companies from Canada, Malaysia, Australia, Italy, South Korea, Turkey, Indonesia and Algeria.
Russia's largest oil company LUKoil and partners Zarubezhneft and Mashinoimport signed in March to develop 7-8 billion barrels of reserves in the southern Qurna oilfield

Potential output capacity from the field is put at 600,000 barrels a day (bpd) but officials said the companies could win rights to the entire southern Iraq Qurna (Qurana) oilfield region, the officials said.
The whole field is believed by Iraq to hold anywhere between 15 and 30 billion barrels.
Mashinoimport is also discussing an agreement for development of the North Rumaila field near the border with Kuwait, the officials said.

Contracted to the former Soviet concern Technoexport prior to the 1990 Gulf crisis the field was scheduled to enter production early in 1992 at an initial rate of 200,000 barrels a day (bpd). Plans were to step up capacity to 500,000 bpd in a subsequent phase.
Russia's fourth largest oil concern Sidanko is the leading contender for a deal to develop the Rafidain field, one of three making up the Charaff exploration axis, the officials said.
Iraqi plans to develop three fields in the region, also including Nasiriya and Gharraf, see output capacity at 390,000 bpd.
Russia's success in securing further Iraqi oil acreage may depend on its investment record in southern Qurna.

Iraq has been encouraging potential oil production partners to sign upstream agreements despite a United Nations ban on investment which will postpone the lion's share of any work until sanctions are lifted.
U.N. sanctions imposed after Baghdad's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait ban investment or trade with Iraq.
Moscow has stressed it will not violate U.N. sanctions. Russian officials said only preliminary feasibility and financing work would begin before sanctions ended.

But Iraqi officials say the Russian companies are obliged to spend $200 million during sanctions on "activities related" to Qurna development and extend a $100 million loan to Iraq for the purchase of equipment.

"The eight billion barrels of reserves amount to about one third of Qurna's total reserves. If Russia honours commitments, it will have the whole Qurna for itself," said one diplomat with close ties to Iraq's oil industry.
"If the Russians go ahead with obligations under the deal they will certainly be given preferential treatment in contracts in areas other than oil," said another diplomat.
China and France also look set for plum contract awards in Iraq.

A delegation from the Chinese National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) is expected soon in Baghdad to lay down the framework for an agreement to develop the billion barrel Ahdab field, the official said.
China also has moved into contention as the leading candidate for the prized Halfaya field in southern Iraq, the official said.
China had recently made a bid for the field, discovered some 20 years ago and believed to hold commercial reserves of about five billion barrels, the official added.
Iraq believes the field could produce some 250,000 barrels a day (bpd) at full capacity.
French Elf Aquitaine and Total already have agreed in principle with Iraq to sign for development respectively of the Majnoon and Nahr Umar fields once sanctions are lifted.
Malaysia's Petronas has been linked with the four billion barrel Ratawi field.
Italy's Agip also is hoping to press its claims for the Halfaya field.
